description: En el espacio profundo la gravedad devuelve NULL, la radiación sube y el cuerpo humano entra en estado crítico. En 200 OK: Still Alive desarrollamos software autónomo de monitoreo médico para detectar anomalías físicas y conductuales antes de que se conviertan en un fallo de misión. Porque a millones de kilómetros de casa, nuestro código se asegura de que la tripulación siempre devuelva un 200 OK
summary: ZENIT is a health monitoring app that helps astronauts understand their own signals and decide what to do next. Simulated smart rings and spacesuit sensors stream readings over a real network connection to a shared crew server. In My health, each astronaut sees their readings, learns whether a sustained change was detected, and gets a plain-language explanation linked to NASA Human Research Program risks, plus a clear next step: add context, recheck, follow a routine or contact the crew medical officer. Astronauts record how they feel, attach captured moments, log follow-ups and can call for help with a deliberate swipe. A crew monitor reviews everyone and manages emergencies. Guided simulations inspired by ARCHeR and Radi-N2, NASA RadLab radiation data and Apollo 11 records explain why monitoring matters in space. Optional Gemini explanations describe the evidence but never diagnose or change the action. Far from Earth, crews must assess their health with limited ground support; ZENIT shows how honest, understandable guidance can make that self-assessment faster and safer
details:
What it does

ZENIT is a crew health monitoring web app built around the question every astronaut asks: "How am I doing, and what should I do next?" It has three parts:

- My health (astronaut view): shows live readings, detects sustained changes, explains them in plain language and suggests a next step. Astronauts record how they feel (activity and recovery, sleep and attention, wellbeing, food and hydration), add symptoms or a note, attach a captured moment and log follow-ups: better, same, worse or contacted crew.

- Crew monitor: a central view of the whole crew with live status, history, saved check-ins and an emergency workflow (active, acknowledged, then resolved with a required note).

- Device simulators: any phone becomes a smart ring (pulse, HRV, SpO₂, respiration, skin temperature deviation) or a spacesuit sensor (ECG pulse, suit pressure, O₂, CO₂, air temperature, battery). A double tap captures a moment; a deliberate swipe sends an emergency.

How it works

Simulators stream readings over WebSockets to a Bun server. The server validates every message, stores it in SQLite and acknowledges an event only after it is saved. Retries never duplicate evidence, and events created offline wait in a queue until they are delivered. ZENIT picks the right source for each mission phase: the ring in Cabin and Recovery, the suit during a Spacewalk. It never substitutes one for the other. When readings stop, they are labelled stale or offline instead of being shown as current. A local, deterministic detector compares recent readings from the same device and phase and selects the next step. Gemini can optionally explain that result using only calculated observations and selected NASA sources. It never receives names or personal notes, and it cannot change the action.

Learning from NASA research

My health connects readings and check-ins to NASA's Human Research Program risks, with a catalogue of 17 topics. Guided simulations inspired by NASA's ARCHeR study (sleep, activity and readiness) and the CSA Radi-N2 experiment (bubble radiation detectors) let astronauts practise interpreting data. Real historical data provides context: 84 DosTel1 radiation observations from NASA OSDR RadLab, and Apollo 11 spacewalk heart-rate records. This data always stays separate from the simulated mission.

Benefits

- Self-assessment without waiting for Earth: explanations, next steps and help prompts run on the crew's own network.

- Honest data: every value shows its source, time and freshness, and missing data is never invented.

- One shared, auditable record for the astronaut and the crew medical officer.

- Clear escalation: a reported concern always outranks reassuring numbers.

Intended impact

On Artemis and future Mars missions, communication delays will make crews more autonomous. ZENIT shows how a health tool can build health literacy, encourage early reporting and keep the crew medical officer informed, while staying clear about what it cannot determine.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript, Svelte 5, SvelteKit 2, Tailwind CSS 4, the Bun runtime, SQLite, WebSockets, Three.js (3D ring model), the Google Gemini API, the NASA OSDR RadLab Data API and Docker. Hardware: ordinary phones, tablets and laptops on the same network; no special devices are required. Automated tests cover the protocol, persistence, detection, AI response validation and interface rendering. AI coding assistants supported development, and the astronaut illustration is AI-generated, as described in our AI-use disclosure.

What makes it creative

- A phone becomes a wearable ring with a simple gesture language: double tap to mark a moment, swipe to call for help.

- Phase-aware sources: the ring and suit act as independent devices that switch with Cabin, Spacewalk and Recovery.

- Learning by practice, with simulations grounded in real NASA and CSA studies.

- AI as an explainer, never the decision-maker.

Factors our team considered

- Safety and honesty: no diagnoses, risk scores or clinical thresholds. Demo triggers are labelled as such. Suit oxygen is not blood oxygen, and radiation stays in μGy/h without being converted into a personal dose.

- Reliability: offline queues, retries that never duplicate data, device and server timestamps, and labels for stale data.

- Privacy: AI requests exclude names and free text, and API keys stay on the server.

- Accessibility: plain English, large touch targets, keyboard support, text labels in addition to colour, and reduced-motion support.

- Limits: biometrics are simulated, and the prototype has no authentication or clinical validation. Real deployment would require validated sensors, approved care pathways and medical review.
